questions.q: For a target precision of epsilon = 0.01, how many classical Monte Carlo samples and how many quantum amplitude estimation oracle queries are needed, per the standard scaling laws?
options: 10,000 classical samples vs. 100 quantum queries
100 classical samples vs. 10,000 quantum queries
1,000 classical samples vs. 1,000 quantum queries
100 classical samples vs. 100 quantum queries
questions.explain: Classical Monte Carlo needs roughly 1/epsilon^2 = 10,000 samples for epsilon=0.01, while quantum amplitude estimation needs roughly 1/epsilon = 100 oracle queries -- a 100x reduction in query count.

questions.q: Why is amplitude estimation's speedup specifically called 'quadratic'?
options: Because quantum query count scales like 1/epsilon while classical sample count scales like 1/epsilon^2 -- quantum queries scale roughly as the square root of classical samples
Because amplitude estimation requires exactly 4 oracle queries regardless of precision
Because the quantum circuit used has exactly 2 qubits
Because classical Monte Carlo always needs twice as many samples as quantum queries
questions.explain: The '1/epsilon vs 1/epsilon^2' relationship means quantum query count is roughly the square root of the classical sample count needed for the same precision, which is the defining signature of a quadratic speedup.

questions.q: Why does the lesson caution that 'quantum needs 1,000x fewer queries' does not mean '1,000x less wall-clock time'?
options: Because each oracle query requires running a real quantum circuit subject to hardware noise and error rates, and building a useful financial oracle circuit is itself nontrivial -- a single quantum query is currently far more expensive than a single classical random sample
Because quantum computers cannot run more than one query per day
Because the 1,000x query reduction number itself is mathematically incorrect
Because classical samples also require building an oracle circuit
questions.explain: A classical random sample can take nanoseconds, while a quantum oracle query requires a real circuit execution with real noise and error rates on current hardware -- so a smaller query count does not automatically translate into a smaller wall-clock time.

questions.q: What does an 'oracle query' refer to in the context of amplitude estimation for risk analysis?
options: One call to a quantum circuit that encodes the probability model (e.g. the simulated distribution of portfolio outcomes) as a quantum state preparation routine
One classical random number generated during a Monte Carlo simulation
A single measurement of a qubit with no circuit execution involved
The final numeric answer returned by the algorithm
questions.explain: An oracle query is one execution of the quantum circuit encoding the financial probability model being estimated -- building that oracle circuit for a realistically complex model is itself a nontrivial engineering challenge.

questions.q: What is the honest gap the lesson identifies between amplitude estimation's theoretical speedup and its practical readiness today?
options: The quadratic speedup is mathematically proven, but realizing its practical benefit requires fault-tolerant quantum hardware well beyond today's scale -- current noisy hardware's error rates and oracle-construction overhead can eliminate the theoretical advantage in practice
The speedup has already been fully demonstrated as faster wall-clock risk calculation on real financial models using today's hardware
There is no gap; amplitude estimation is purely theoretical and has no proven mathematical basis at all
The speedup only applies to classical computers, not quantum ones
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes a proven theoretical speedup from a demonstrated practical one -- current hardware's noise and the overhead of building useful oracle circuits mean this speedup's real-world benefit for financial risk analysis remains unproven today, mirroring Chapter 5's broader benchmarking theme.
